questions.stem: The MOST WIDELY distributed soil in India is:

options.option_text: Red soil
Alluvial soil
Black (regur) soil
Laterite soil

questions.explanation: Alluvial soil covers ~43% of India (~144 million ha), chiefly the Northern Plains (Indo-Gangetic) and river deltas. Most fertile — rich in potash, phosphoric acid, lime. Ideal for rice, wheat, sugarcane, pulses.

questions.stem: BLACK SOIL (Regur) is best suited for which CROP?

options.option_text: Rice
Cotton
Tea
Jute

questions.explanation: Black soil (regur) — also called 'black cotton soil'. Formed from Deccan basalt. Rich in iron, magnesium, calcium; high moisture-retention. Found in Maharashtra, MP, Gujarat, Karnataka. Rice/jute need alluvial + water; tea needs laterite hill-slopes with acidic pH.

questions.stem: Match the AGRICULTURAL REVOLUTION with its focus. A. Green Revolution.  B. White Revolution.  C. Blue Revolution.  D. Yellow Revolution. List-II: 1. Foodgrains (wheat / rice).  2. Milk.  3. Fisheries / aquaculture.  4. Oilseeds.
questions.explanation: Green — foodgrains (Swaminathan). White — milk (Kurien's Operation Flood). Blue — fisheries (Hiralal Chaudhuri credited for induced fish breeding). Yellow — oilseeds (Sam Pitroda coined the term). Bonus: Pink — prawns/onions; Silver — eggs/poultry; Golden — fruits / horticulture / honey; Round — potato.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a RABI crop?

options.option_text: Rice
Wheat
Jute
Cotton

questions.explanation: Rabi — sown in winter (Oct-Dec), harvested in spring/summer (Apr-Jun). Wheat, barley, gram, mustard, peas, lentils. Kharif — sown June-July (monsoon), harvested Sep-Oct. Rice, jute, cotton, maize, millets. Zaid — summer season between rabi and kharif (watermelon, cucumber).

questions.stem: India is the LARGEST producer in the world of:

options.option_text: Wheat
Jute, milk and pulses
Rice
Coffee

questions.explanation: India is #1 globally in milk (since 1998, Operation Flood), pulses, jute, mangoes, bananas, spices. China beats India in wheat and rice. Brazil leads in coffee. Ranking can shift slightly year-on-year, but jute-milk-pulses is a very stable #1 combo.

questions.stem: The Minimum Support Price (MSP) for agricultural crops in India is recommended by:

options.option_text: Food Corporation of India
Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)
NITI Aayog
Ministry of Agriculture directly

questions.explanation: CACP (est. 1965, then 'Agricultural Prices Commission') — recommends MSPs for 22 mandated crops (7 cereals, 5 pulses, 7 oilseeds + toria, copra, cotton, raw jute). The CCEA approves. FCI handles procurement and storage of rice and wheat.

questions.stem: 'Bangar' and 'Khadar' are the two sub-types of which major soil group found in India?

options.option_text: Black cotton soil, found mainly in the Deccan Plateau
Alluvial soil, deposited by rivers in the Indo-Gangetic plain
Red and yellow soil, common in Eastern Peninsular India
Laterite soil, formed by leaching in high-rainfall regions

questions.explanation: Alluvial soil is divided into Bangar (older, higher terraces, more kankar nodules) and Khadar (newer, lower flood plains, finer and more fertile). Black soil has no such sub-division; laterite and red soils are associated with peninsular uplands, not river plains.

questions.stem: Which among the following is correctly categorised as a 'Zaid' crop in India's agricultural calendar?

options.option_text: Wheat, a cool-season cereal harvested in March and April
Watermelon, cultivated in the short summer inter-season period
Paddy (rice), sown at the onset of the southwest monsoon
Mustard, an oilseed crop harvested mainly in February–March

questions.explanation: Zaid (or Zayad) crops are grown in the short warm season between the Rabi harvest and the Kharif sowing (roughly March–June). Watermelon, muskmelon, and cucumber are classic Zaid crops. Wheat and mustard are Rabi; paddy is the chief Kharif crop. The distractor 'mustard in February' tempts candidates who know its harvest timing but confuse harvest month with crop season.

questions.stem: Which soil type in India is said to have a 'self-ploughing' or 'self-mulching' property owing to alternate wetting and drying?

options.option_text: Alluvial soil, highly fertile and found in river floodplains
Laterite soil, which hardens irreversibly on exposure to air
Vertisol (Black soil), which shrinks and cracks deeply when dry
Red soil, which is deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus, and humus

questions.explanation: Vertisols (Black/Regur soils) are rich in montmorillonite clay, which expands greatly when wet and contracts with wide, deep cracks when dry. Plant material falls into the cracks and gets mixed into the soil — hence 'self-ploughing'. Laterite (Option B) also hardens on exposure but does not crack and is the most tempting wrong answer because candidates associate both soils with seasonal rainfall areas.

questions.stem: Darjeeling Tea is widely cited as India's first product to receive a Geographical Indication (GI) tag. In which year was this registration formally granted?

options.option_text: 2003 — the year the GI Act (1999) came into operational force
2004 — registered as GI-1 under the GI of Goods Act, 1999
2007 — when India acceded to the Lisbon Agreement on appellations
2009 — coinciding with India's entry into the Madrid Protocol

questions.explanation: The GI of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 came into force on 15 September 2003, but the first registration — GI Application No. 1 — was granted to Darjeeling Tea in October 2004. Option A (2003) is the most common mistake because candidates conflate when the Act became operative with when the first tag was actually issued.

questions.stem: In tribal communities of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, shifting cultivation is locally known as 'Podu'. What is its counterpart name used predominantly in the Northeastern hill states?

options.option_text: Bewar — the term used in Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh hills
Jhum — the term used across Assam, Nagaland, and Mizoram
Waltre — the term used in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
Dahiya — the term used in Bundelkhand region of Madhya Pradesh

questions.explanation: Shifting cultivation goes by regional names: Jhum (Northeast India), Podu (AP/Odisha), Bewar or Dahiya (MP/Chhattisgarh), Ponam (Kerala), and Kumari (Western Ghats). 'Jhum' is the PYQ-frequent term because Northeast tribal land rights and Jhum cycles appear in forest policy questions. Bewar (Option A) is a real alternate name but belongs to MP, not the Northeast — a classic trap.

questions.stem: According to the USDA Soil Taxonomy adopted by NBSS&LUP, which soil ORDER covers the LARGEST geographical area in India, accounting for nearly 40% of the country's land?

options.option_text: Vertisols — shrink-swell black soils concentrated in the Deccan
Inceptisols — young, weakly developed soils widespread across India
Entisols — minimal-profile soils in recent alluvial and desert zones
Alfisols — moderately leached soils under seasonally dry deciduous tracts

questions.explanation: NBSS&LUP data places Inceptisols as India's dominant soil order (~39.74%), found across the Himalayan foothills, Northeastern plains, and parts of the peninsula where soil formation is active but horizon differentiation is still weak. Entisols (~28%) are second. Vertisols, though iconic in GK questions, cover only ~8.5%. Most candidates incorrectly choose Entisols because alluvial soils are the 'most widespread' in popular GK, but alluvial soils span both Entisol and Inceptisol orders in the USDA system.

questions.stem: Under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY), which of the following risks is specifically EXCLUDED from the standard insurance coverage?

options.option_text: Prevented sowing losses caused by deficit rainfall or excess flooding
Mid-season adversity losses from prolonged dry spells or severe drought
Crop damage arising from war, nuclear hazards, or willful farmer neglect
Post-harvest losses occurring within two weeks of cutting for field drying

questions.explanation: PMFBY (launched 2016) is comprehensive: it covers prevented sowing (Option A), mid-season adversities (Option B), post-harvest losses up to a fortnight after harvest (Option D), and localised calamities like hailstorm and landslide. However, losses due to war, nuclear risk, malicious damage, and willful negligence by the insured are standard exclusions under all government crop insurance schemes. Option D is the most tempting because post-harvest coverage is a lesser-known feature of PMFBY that candidates assume is excluded.
